content: 1. Following the 2010 guidelines, all countries except one have adopted the recommended practices for HIV-infected mothers and infant feeding. 2. Regarding infant feeding practices for mothers living with HIV, 19 out of 21 countries recommend breastfeeding with antiretroviral (ARV) interventions for all HIV-infected mothers. Only two countries adopt an individualized approach based on the mother’s condition. None of the countries recommend avoiding breastfeeding entirely for HIV-infected mothers. 3. Option B+ (lifelong maternal triple ARV treatment) is recommended in 19 countries. However, two of these countries reported that parts of their regions are still transitioning from Option A to Option B+. Two other countries recommend Option B (maternal triple ARV drugs during pregnancy and breastfeeding), with one of them beginning to implement Option B+ in certain areas. 4. In some cases, the implementation of Option B+ began before the complete revision of national guidelines, leading to inconsistencies in the documentation of recommendations. 5. All countries recommend exclusive breastfeeding for HIV-infected mothers until six months of age. In 18 countries, breastfeeding is advised to continue from six to 12 months, while two countries recommend extending breastfeeding up to 24 months. One country promotes exclusive breastfeeding until six months, followed by infant formula from six to 12 months. 6. In countries with individualized approaches, mothers who choose not to breastfeed are advised to use infant formula from birth to 12 months (two countries) or modified animal milk (one country). 7. The ARV drugs recommended for Options B+ and B are tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), lamivudine/emtricitabine (3TC/FTC), and efavirenz (EFV). Four countries use alternative regimens, such as zidovudine (AZT), lamivudine, and lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r), or AZT, lamivudine, and nevirapine (NVP). One country offers a third alternative: AZT, lamivudine, and abacavir. 8. In countries still using Option A, the ARV regimen includes AZT starting at 14 weeks of gestation or as soon as possible, AZT/3TC/NVP during delivery, and AZT/3TC for seven days postpartum. In Mozambique, both AZT and NVP are used. 9. The most recent revisions of maternal ARV regimens occurred in 2012 for one country and between 2013 and 2015 for others. One country could not specify the date of its last update. 10. Exclusive breastfeeding until six months is universally recommended. After six months, 18 countries advise continued breastfeeding until 12 months, while two recommend extending it to 24 months. One country suggests exclusive breastfeeding until six months, followed by infant formula until 12 months. 11. For HIV-positive infants, recommendations are generally the same as for HIV-negative or status-unknown infants in seven countries. Eleven countries promote breastfeeding until 24 months instead of 12 months or formula feeding until 12 months. One country has no specific recommendations for this case. 12. The recommendation for HIV-infected mothers to breastfeed for 24 months is already being implemented in some facilities in two countries. Respondents reported no major difficulties in implementation, except for challenges related to training time and resources. 13. In half of the countries, health workers find the acceptability and feasibility of promoting 24-month breastfeeding to be difficult or somewhat difficult, while the other half find it easy or very easy. One country was uncertain about what to expect. 14. The main concerns regarding the acceptability and feasibility of 24-month breastfeeding include resistance from health workers and mothers due to fears of HIV transmission, especially if ARV adherence is inconsistent. Some health workers are uncomfortable with breastfeeding beyond six months, citing increased transmission risk. Scientific evidence and training are needed to address these concerns. 15. Heat treatment of expressed breast milk is included in the guidelines of half the countries. Circumstances for heat treatment include when the mother is unwell or has temporary breast health issues (e.g., mastitis), when the infant is ill or of low birth weight, to assist mothers in stopping breastfeeding, or if ARVs are temporarily unavailable. 16. Most countries do not specify recommendations for situations where ARVs are unavailable or interrupted. 17. Counseling approaches for HIV-infected mothers on infant feeding vary. Some countries recommend individual counseling, while others combine group and individual counseling. A few countries provide no specific recommendations. 18. The International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes is implemented through legislation in 16 countries and voluntary measures in one. Four countries reported no implementation. 19. Technical advisory groups on HIV and infant feeding exist in most countries, either as dedicated groups or integrated into broader groups such as PMTCT, IYCF, or nutrition committees. 20. All national working plans on HIV and infant feeding have been updated since 2010. However, three plans are not costed, and none are fully funded. 21. Postpartum follow-up care protocols for HIV-infected mothers and their infants are integrated into various plans in most countries. Viral load testing is the least frequently included support, though more than 50% of countries offer it. 22. Infant ARV prophylaxis protocols include NVP for six weeks in most countries. Other regimens include NVP for 12 weeks, NVP+AZT for four weeks, or AZT syrup for six weeks. Special recommendations include switching to triple ARVs if the infant shows HIV symptoms or using NVP instead of AZT for anemic infants. 23. Virological testing (PCR) at birth is being implemented in one country, with feasibility considered easy. Other countries anticipate challenges in implementation. 24. Infant HIV testing at routine immunization and growth monitoring clinics is being implemented in eight countries, with feasibility considered easy. Other countries expect difficulties. 25. All 21 surveyed countries have conducted training courses on HIV and infant feeding, either as standalone courses or integrated into broader training programs. Most courses were updated after 2010, with the last training occurring less than a year ago in most countries.
